extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, filmmakers, and fiction writers interested in story craft and screenwriting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing climaxes, resolutions, antagonistic forces, and exposition in screenplays and narrative fiction so scenes and character arcs build to an inevitable-yet-unexpected payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes must be justified by the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Work back from the ending to make certain that by Idea and Counter-Idea every image, beat, action, or line of dialogue somehow relates to or sets up this grand payoff. All scenes must be thematically or structurally justified in the light of the Climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a scene can be cut without disturbing the impact of the ending, it must be cut. Every scene should either build toward or foreshadow the Climax; keep only scenes that contribute to the thematic/structural payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax subplots should climax within or build to the Central Climax
rubrics_metrics.description: If logic allows, climax subplots within the Central Plot’s Climax so one final action by the protagonist can settle multiple threads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When impossible, climax the least important subplots earliest, then the next most important, building overall to the Central Plot’s Climax. Prefer a multiplying effect where one climactic action resolves several subplots (example: Rick in CASABLANCA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the audience the emotion promised, but not the way it expects
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer determines what emotion will satisfy the audience at the end by the way the story is told; deliver that emotion but in an unexpected manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences want emotional satisfaction (not necessarily a happy ending). Promise a particular emotional outcome through the telling, and then fulfill it with surprise — the difference between artist and amateur (William Goldman principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: An ending must be both inevitable and unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: In Aristotle’s words: an ending must be 'inevitable and unexpected' — inevitable because, in retrospect, the telling shows the Climax was the only path; unexpected because it occurs in a way the audience could not have anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the Climax feel like the natural outcome of the story’s given characters and world while structuring a Turning Point within the Climax (a withheld insight or Gap) that shocks and recontextualizes prior events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a Turning Point within the Climax (the Gap/insight)
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist gives the promised emotion with a rush of unexpected insight withheld until a Turning Point within the Climax itself, so the protagonist’s final improvisation may or may not achieve the desire, but delivers the emotion in a way we could never have foreseen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the Climax so a key piece of insight (a Gap) re-frames the story, sending the audience back through the telling with fresh understanding (example: LOVE SERENADE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a Key Image that concentrates meaning and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Truffaut’s 'Spectacle and Truth': create the Key Image of the film — a single image that sums up and concentrates all meaning and emotion; like the coda of a symphony, it echoes what has gone before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the climax for the eye as well as theme; aim for a visual, memorable Key Image that when recalled returns the whole film to the audience (examples: GREED in McTeague, TREASURE OF THE SIERRA MADRE, LA DOLCE VITA, SLING BLADE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution should be used sparingly and with purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Resolution (material after Climax) has three uses: climaxing leftover subplots, showing the spread of climactic effects across society/supporting cast, or providing a 'slow curtain' so the audience can catch its breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid awkward end scenes of secondary interest; if needed, tie the Resolution back to the Central Plot (example: THE IN-LAWS comedic false twist) or show social consequences (parties, title rolls) and provide a brief breathing-out sequence rather than abrupt blackout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Antagonism: antagonism sets the scale of character and story
rubrics_metrics.description: A protagonist and his story can only be as intellectually fascinating and emotionally compelling as the forces of antagonism make them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design strong, complex, and multi-level antagonistic forces (internal, interpersonal, institutional, environmental) so the protagonist is an underdog with a real chance but not certainty; stronger antagonism yields deeper character realization and a more compelling climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonism must explore degrees from Contrary to Contradictory to Negation of the Negation
rubrics_metrics.description: A story that progresses to the limit of human experience in depth and breadth of conflict must move through a pattern that includes the Contrary, the Contradictory, and the Negation of the Negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the negative progression of the core value at stake (e.g., Justice → Unfairness → Injustice → Tyranny) and push some element to the Negation of the Negation (the end of the line) to achieve brilliance rather than mere satisfactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the primary value at stake and chart its negative declension
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by identifying the primary value (e.g., Justice, Love, Truth) and weigh Positive, Contrary, Contradictory, and Negation of the Negation to test whether your antagonism reaches the end of the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use value-mapping (Positive → Contrary → Contradictory → Negation of the Negation) to self-critique: does the story explore all shades of negativity? Does it reach a qualitatively worse state when needed? Examples in text cover Love, Truth, Consciousness, Wealth, Communication, Success, Intelligence, Liberty, Courage, Loyalty, Maturity, and Sexual sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose weak stories by weak forces of antagonism
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story seems unsatisfying and lacking, the inevitable cause is that forces of antagonism are weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than inventing more likable protagonist traits, pour creativity into strengthening the negative side (increasing stakes, complexity, and depth of opposition) to produce a chain reaction that pays off in the climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell — dramatize exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition is the information the audience needs about setting, biography, and characterization. Well-done exposition makes this knowledge invisible; dramatize exposition so it further the immediate conflict first and convey information second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never force characters to state facts they both know without a compelling motivation. Convert exposition to ammunition (facts used as tools/attacks in the struggle) so information is passed naturally through conflict and behavior rather than flat telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only give exposition that is necessary for comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Never include anything the audience can reasonably and easily assume has happened. Never pass on exposition unless the missing fact would cause confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withhold information to maintain interest; reveal secrets deliberately. The least important facts should come early, more important later, and critical facts (secrets) last — some exposition may be revealed well into the Climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace exposition progressively with secrets last
rubrics_metrics.description: Pace the exposition so the least important facts come early, the next most important later, and the critical facts last. Critical pieces of exposition are secrets—the painful truths characters do not want known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure revelation as a progression; do not dump essential facts up front. Secrets may be withheld until late, even into the Climax, to preserve tension and payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'California scenes' — unmotivated telling between strangers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'California scenes': scenes where two characters who hardly know each other exchange intimate biographical confessions with no truthful motivation are forced and false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information is needed, create a stronger scene motivation than the facts themselves. Authentic reveal must arise from credible dramatic necessity, not contrived conversation that exists solely to inform the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing is not montage-telling; prefer truthful character and camera behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Show, don't tell' does not mean ordering a camera to pan a mantelpiece of photos to summarize history; that's telling, not showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters and camera behave truthfully in scenes that dramatize exposition; avoid turning a film into a home movie via summarizing devices that short-circuit dramatic living of events.
